newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S DENEL STILL TRYING TO SELL TO MALAYSIA.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S DENEL STILL TRYING TO SELL TO MALAYSIA.

text.p: South Africa's Denel arms maker said on Thursday it was still trying to persuade Malaysia to buy its Rooivalk helicopter and no deal had been signed yet.

"We know that the Malaysians are interested, we know they have made positive sounds," Denel chief executive Johan Alberts said in an interview at a maritime defence exhibition at the Simonstown navy base.
"But there are still a lot of things we must do before we can say it is signed and sealed... We're going to work towards it."
Alberts said he did not know how many of the aircraft Malaysia was interested in buying.
Malaysia's national news agency Bernama last week quoted Defence Minister Syed Hamid Albar as saying the country wanted to buy eight but that the deal was still being negotiated.
The Simonstown defence exhibition is being held as part of celebrations to mark the 75th anniversary of the South African navy. Ships or representatives from about 30 countries are attending.
Alberts said Denel was hoping the U.S. state department would finally lift a denial order barring U.S. companies from dealing with South Africa.

The ban was imposed after the United States accused Denel and associated companies of illegally obtaining U.S. military technology during the 1980s, but earlier this year South Africa agreed to pay fines to settle the dispute.
"Before we start (dealing with American companies) we've got to find out from the clients whether they are willing to work with the American companies," he said.
"When you form alliances... the customers are sometimes dedicated to certain philosophies and they wouldn't like another supplier to get into the deal."
Asked if getting the legal go-ahead to fit U.S. kit to the Rooivalk would help sales of the aircraft, Alberts said:
"Only if the customer would like us to do that. We know that we can integrate American equipment. If the client requires that, and the Americans are willing, we can do that."
He said some of Denel's clients were "sensitive" about buying U.S. equipment. "We never question their reasons."
Alberts said Denel was not only a manufacturer but could also advise clients on strategy and applications with a view to making the best use of their military resources.

"That's the name of the game nowadays with the steep decline in defence budgets. By doing that, as a small player in the international market Denel can do a lot, we can enhance our business," he said.
Alberts said Denel was operating in more than 100 countries and had sales contracts with 70 or 80.

Among the exhibitors at the Simonstown show are shipbuilders which tendered two years ago to provide South Africa with four corvettes -- Bazan of Spain, Yarrow of Britain, the German Frigate Consortium, and DCN International of France.
Bazan was identified at the time as the favoured company but negotiations were frozen pending a South African defence review which is due to establish what new equipment the country can afford.
"We hope we still get the contract, but we know nothing definite," said Bazan spokesman Miguel Martinez.
A Yarrow spokesman said the shipyards were at the exhibition to show they were still interested. "We're here flying the flag," he said.
-- Anton Ferreira, Cape Town newsroom +2721 252-238
